title: Phishing Email Deception
body:
EDUCATION. Phishing is deception by email: a message pretends to come from someone the reader trusts, such as a bank, a delivery company, or a colleague, and tries to move the reader to click a link, open an attachment, or hand over credentials. It works because email was designed to carry text, not proof of identity, so a sender name on screen is only a claim until it is checked. The standard checks are sender authentication records that let a receiving server verify whether the sending server is authorized for the claimed domain, and whether the message content was altered in transit. When those checks fail or are absent, the message deserves suspicion no matter how familiar it looks. Teaching this class starts with one habit: treat every unexpected request in email as unverified until an independent check confirms it.

INFORMATION AWARENESS. Recognize phishing by its tells: a sender domain that is close to but not exactly the trusted domain, urgency language that pushes immediate action, a link whose visible text names one destination while its real destination points elsewhere, an unexpected attachment, and a request for a password or a code that a legitimate service would not ask for by email. Documented real cases include a 2013 retail breach that began with deceptive mail sent to a vendor, and the widely reported 2016 political campaign intrusions that began with deceptive credential-harvesting mail. Indicators of compromise for defenders include authentication failures on inbound mail, spikes in reports to the abuse mailbox, and credential-use anomalies after a mail wave. Awareness training that uses realistic samples, reported honestly and without punishment, measurably raises reporting rates.

SOLUTIONS. Cure and immunization: publish and enforce sender authentication for your own domains so others can verify your mail; reject or quarantine inbound mail that fails authentication; filter known malicious senders and newly registered lookalike domains; require multi-factor authentication so a stolen password alone does not open an account. Fix and response playbook: when a wave is reported, quarantine the messages, warn recipients, force password resets for anyone who submitted credentials, revoke active sessions, and review sign-in logs for misuse. Resistance verification: run the header analyzer in this record's demo against labeled samples and require it to flag every deceptive sample while passing every legitimate one before the rule is trusted in production.

title: Smishing and Vishing Deception
body:
EDUCATION. Smishing is phishing by text message and vishing is phishing by voice call. Both work the same way as email phishing, but they exploit two extra weaknesses: a phone number on a screen feels personal, and a live voice creates social pressure that a written message does not. The attacker impersonates a bank, a delivery service, a government office, or a colleague, then creates urgency, a missed parcel, a locked account, an unpaid toll, and asks the target to tap a link, call a number, or read back a code. No legitimate organization asks for a password, a one-time code, or remote access to a device through an unsolicited text or call, and that single rule defeats most of these attempts before any technology is involved.

INFORMATION AWARENESS. Recognize smishing by short links, misspelled sender names, unexpected parcel or toll notices, and any request to tap now. Recognize vishing by a caller who refuses to let you hang up and call back on a published number, who asks for codes or remote access, or who uses background noise and authority to rush you. Documented real waves include bank-impersonation text campaigns and tax-office impersonation call campaigns reported by consumer protection agencies in many countries. Indicators for defenders include clusters of reports naming the same sender number or link domain, and help-desk tickets about unexpected verification codes. Awareness means teaching one behavior above all: hang up, do not tap, and contact the organization through a number or address you already trust.

SOLUTIONS. Cure and immunization: block reported sender numbers and link domains at the carrier or gateway level where available; filter messages carrying known lure phrases; teach staff and family the hang-up-and-call-back rule; never read back a one-time code to an inbound caller. Fix and response playbook: when a wave is reported, warn the targeted group with the exact lure text, block the sender, report the number and domain to the carrier and to the relevant fraud reporting service, and review accounts for anyone who complied. title: Weak and Reused Passwords
body:
EDUCATION. Password attacks succeed most often without any cleverness at all: the attacker simply tries passwords that people actually use, or tries passwords stolen from one service against many others. Short passwords fall to automated guessing, common passwords fall to lists of the most used passwords, and reused passwords turn one breach into many, because a password leaked from a minor service opens the victim's mail, banking, and work accounts if it is the same string everywhere. The defense is not a more complicated password alone; it is length, uniqueness per service, and a second factor that a stolen password cannot satisfy. A password manager exists precisely to make long unique passwords practical for ordinary people.

INFORMATION AWARENESS. Recognize the risk by checking three facts: is the password short, is it a common word or pattern, and is it used anywhere else. Documented real cases include a 2012 social network breach whose leaked password hashes later fueled credential-stuffing waves against unrelated services, and the long public history of breached-password lists traded openly. Indicators of compromise include sign-in attempts from many locations against many accounts, a sudden rise in failed logins, and successful logins from unfamiliar devices shortly after a known breach elsewhere. Awareness means treating every breach notice as a prompt to change that password everywhere it was reused, not only on the breached service.

SOLUTIONS. Cure and immunization: require passwords of at least twelve characters; reject known breached and common passwords at creation; require a unique password per service, supported by a password manager; require multi-factor authentication on every important account, especially mail, which resets the others. Fix and response playbook: when a service reports a breach, change that password everywhere it was reused, revoke sessions, turn on multi-factor authentication, and check account activity for misuse. Resistance verification: run the policy evaluator in this record's demo against sample passwords and require it to reject every weak or reused sample while accepting every strong unique one before the policy is trusted.

title: Malicious USB and Removable Media
body:
EDUCATION. Removable media attacks work by exploiting trust in a physical object: a found drive, a gifted drive, or a vendor's drive is plugged into a computer that then trusts it. The risk is not only files on the drive; a computer that automatically runs content from inserted media, or that trusts any inserted device as a keyboard or network adapter, hands control to whatever the device claims to be. The defense is therefore a device policy, not vigilance alone: decide in advance which devices are allowed, block the rest, never run content automatically from removable media, and scan allowed media before use. Physical security and device policy are the same control viewed from two sides.

INFORMATION AWARENESS. Recognize the risk by its setting: an unattended drive in a car park or lobby, an unsolicited drive received by post, a borrowed drive of unknown origin, and any prompt to run content from inserted media. The documented real case most often cited is a 2010 industrial incident in which removable media carried malicious code into an isolated network, a case studied publicly ever since as the reason air gaps need device policy, not just separation. Indicators of compromise include unexpected autorun prompts, new devices appearing in logs on machines that should accept none, and security software alerts on inserted media. Awareness means one rule for everyone: never plug in media you did not expect from a source you trust, and report found media to security instead of testing it.

SOLUTIONS. Cure and immunization: disable autorun and autoplay for removable media on every machine; allow only registered devices by hardware identifier and block all others; require scanning of allowed media before files are opened; encrypt sensitive data on approved media so a lost drive leaks nothing readable. Fix and response playbook: when an unknown device is inserted, remove it, preserve logs, scan the machine, check for new programs and scheduled tasks, and treat the machine as suspect until the scan is clean. Resistance verification: run the device-policy checker in this record's demo against sample devices and require it to block every unregistered device while admitting every registered, scanned one before the policy is trusted.

title: Unpatched Software Exposure
body:
EDUCATION. Unpatched software is the most reliably exploited weakness in computing, because a published fix is also a public announcement of the flaw: once a vendor ships a patch, the difference between the old and new code tells every reader exactly where the old version was vulnerable. Systems that stay unpatched therefore remain open to anyone who reads the advisory. The defense is a patching discipline, not a single update: know what software you run, learn about fixes promptly, test them, and install them on a schedule that treats internet-facing and widely used software first. Patching is also the cheapest defense available, since the vendor has already done the hard work of finding and fixing the flaw.

INFORMATION AWARENESS. Recognize exposure by comparing installed versions against the vendor's fixed versions, and by watching advisories for the software you run. Documented real cases include a 2017 credit-reporting breach traced to an unpatched web framework component, and a 2017 worm outbreak that spread through an unpatched file-sharing service months after the fix shipped. Indicators of compromise include exploitation attempts against old versions visible in logs, and inventory reports showing widely deployed versions below the fixed version. Awareness means treating a patch advisory as a countdown: the window between publication and mass exploitation is measured in days, sometimes hours, for widely used software.

SOLUTIONS. Cure and immunization: maintain a complete software inventory; subscribe to vendor advisories for everything in it; patch internet-facing systems first and on a fixed cadence; remove software you no longer need so it cannot stay unpatched unnoticed. Fix and response playbook: when a critical advisory lands, identify every affected system, apply the fix or apply the vendor's workaround if no fix exists yet, verify the new version is running, and hunt logs for exploitation attempts during the exposure window. title: Open Wi-Fi Eavesdropping
body:
EDUCATION. Open Wi-Fi eavesdropping works because radio is a shared medium: anything a device sends over an unencrypted wireless network can be received by any other device in range that listens. On a network without encryption, or where only the network password is shared, traffic that is not itself encrypted is readable to a listener, including session tokens that let a listener impersonate the user on a site. The defense is to encrypt the traffic itself rather than trusting the network: use sites and apps that encrypt end to end, prefer networks with individual encryption, and use a virtual private network on networks you do not control. The network is a road; encryption is the sealed envelope.

INFORMATION AWARENESS. Recognize the risk by the network's character: a network with no password, a network whose password is printed on a wall, a network name that imitates a legitimate venue, and any warning from the device about the connection. The classic public demonstration, in 2010, showed session tokens being collected over open networks, which is why session protection is now standard on major sites. Indicators of compromise include sessions hijacked after public network use, logins from unfamiliar locations, and duplicate network names appearing near a venue. Awareness means one rule: treat every network you do not control as hostile to unencrypted traffic, and never do sensitive work over it without encryption.

title: Social Engineering Pretexting
body:
EDUCATION. Pretexting is lying with a story: the attacker invents a role, an emergency, and an authority, then uses the story to make a helpful person hand over information or access. title: SQL Injection by Input Concatenation
body:
EDUCATION. SQL injection is a flaw in how an application builds database commands: when user input is pasted directly into a command string, the input stops being data and starts being instructions. A database cannot tell which part of the finished string the programmer wrote and which part the user supplied, so input shaped like a command fragment changes what the command does, typically by widening a lookup to return rows it should not, or by altering data. The cure is structural, not a filter: the command is sent with placeholders, and user input is sent separately as values only, so the database never treats input as instructions. Parameterized queries are the standard form of this separation, and they defeat the whole class rather than one spelling of it.

INFORMATION AWARENESS. Recognize the risk wherever an application builds database commands from user input: login forms, search boxes, filters, and identifiers passed in web addresses. The class has been a staple of public vulnerability lists since the 2000s and appears in documented breaches across decades, which is why it remains a first check in every application review. Indicators of compromise include database errors shown to users, unusual query patterns in logs such as unexpected wildcards or always-true conditions, and data returned to users who should not see it. Awareness for reviewers means one question asked of every query: is user input ever concatenated into the command string, or does it always travel as a parameter.

Cure and immunization: require parameterized queries or a vetted data-access layer everywhere; forbid string concatenation of user input into commands in code review; give the application's database account only the permissions it needs, so even a flaw cannot reach unrelated tables; hide database errors from users. title: Cross-Site Scripting in Web Pages
body:
EDUCATION. Cross-site scripting is a flaw in how an application prints user-supplied content into a web page: when content is inserted without encoding, the browser cannot tell which part of the page the programmer wrote and which part a user supplied, so supplied content shaped like page code runs as page code in other visitors' browsers. The running code acts with the victim's session, which is why stored variants that persist on the site are more dangerous than reflected variants that need a crafted link. The cure is again structural: encode output for its context, so supplied text is always displayed as text and never interpreted as code, and add a content-security policy that limits which scripts a page may run at all.

INFORMATION AWARENESS. Recognize the risk wherever a site echoes user content: comments, profiles, search results, and error pages that repeat input. The classic public case is a 2005 social-network worm that spread through profile content, a case still taught because it showed a stored flaw becoming self-propagating. Indicators of compromise include unexpected scripts in stored content, user reports of strange behavior on specific pages, and session anomalies after visits to a poisoned page. Awareness for reviewers means one question asked of every place user content is printed: is it encoded for exactly the context it lands in, HTML text, an attribute, or a script block, since each context needs different encoding.

title: Broken Access Control
body:
EDUCATION. Broken access control is the flaw where an application checks that a user is logged in but not whether that user is allowed to do the requested thing. A logged-in user who asks for another user's record, an administrative function, or a hidden step in a workflow gets it, because the application never asks the authorization question. It works because developers naturally test the allowed path and forget the forbidden ones. The cure is to enforce authorization on the server for every request, using the authenticated user's identity and the requested object's ownership, and to deny by default: anything not explicitly allowed is refused. Client-side hiding of buttons is presentation, not control, and must never be mistaken for it.

INFORMATION AWARENESS. Recognize the risk wherever identifiers appear in requests: record numbers, file names, account references, and workflow steps that can be reached directly. The class topped the 2021 edition of a widely used public vulnerability list and appears constantly in public bug-bounty reports, which is why it is a first check in application reviews. Indicators of compromise include access logs showing users reaching records they do not own, direct requests to administrative paths from ordinary accounts, and data appearing in accounts that never created it. Awareness for testers means one habit: for every function, try it as a user who should be refused, not only as one who should be allowed.

SOLUTIONS. Cure and immunization: enforce server-side authorization on every endpoint; use ownership and role checks, not obscurity; deny by default; log authorization failures and alert on spikes. title: Ransomware File Encryption
body:
EDUCATION. Ransomware is malicious software that encrypts a victim's files and demands payment for the key, and its power comes from a simple asymmetry: encryption is fast and total, while recovery without a key is infeasible. Modern variants also steal data first and threaten to publish it, so even victims with backups face extortion. The attack typically arrives through deceptive mail, an unpatched service, or a stolen account, then spreads to reachable shares and backups. title: Man-in-the-Middle and Session Hijacking
body:
EDUCATION. A man-in-the-middle attack inserts the attacker between a user and a service so traffic passes through hostile hands, and session hijacking is its most common prize: stealing the session token that proves a user is logged in, then presenting it as the user's own. It works where traffic is unencrypted, where a network is hostile, or where session tokens leak into logs, addresses, or unprotected storage. The defense is to make the session token useless to anyone but its owner: send it only over encrypted connections, mark it so scripts cannot read it, bind its use to the encrypted channel, and expire it promptly. title: Privilege Escalation by Misconfiguration
body:
EDUCATION. Privilege escalation by misconfiguration happens when an ordinary account can reach more power than it should because permissions were set too broadly: a shared folder anyone can write to, a service running with excessive rights, a script anyone can edit that a privileged account runs, or a cloud role with permissions far beyond its job. The attacker needs no new flaw; the system itself hands over the ladder. The defense is least privilege as a discipline: every account, service, and role gets exactly the permissions its job requires and nothing more, permissions are reviewed on a schedule, and powerful operations are separated from everyday work. Misconfiguration is the most common escalation path precisely because it is created by defenders, not discovered by attackers.

INFORMATION AWARENESS. Recognize the risk by auditing for breadth: groups named everyone or authenticated users holding write or full control, services running as system-level accounts when a lesser account would do, scheduled tasks and scripts writable by ordinary users, and cloud roles carrying administrative permissions for narrow jobs. Indicators of compromise include permission changes outside change control, new accounts or role assignments, and ordinary accounts performing administrative actions. Awareness means treating a permission audit as a security control with an owner and a cadence, not a one-time cleanup.

title: DNS Spoofing and Cache Poisoning
body:
EDUCATION. DNS spoofing and cache poisoning attack the phone book of the internet: when a device asks where a name lives, a forged answer can send it to an attacker's server instead. Cache poisoning plants the forged answer in a resolver's memory so many users are misdirected at once. It works because early DNS trusted answers without proof of origin, and because a resolver that accepts the first plausible answer can be raced with forgeries. The defenses are proof and unpredictability: signed answers that a resolver can verify, unpredictable query identifiers and ports that make racing hard, and encrypted transport that hides queries from listeners. A name that cannot be verified should not be trusted.

INFORMATION AWARENESS. Recognize the risk by its symptoms: users reaching lookalike sites for familiar names, certificate warnings on well-known services, and resolver logs showing conflicting answers. The classic public research in 2008 showed cache poisoning was practical at scale and drove the adoption of the defenses above. A documented public campaign in 2019 redirected traffic by abusing DNS records, showing the class remains live. Indicators of compromise include unexpected address changes for high-value names, resolver cache entries that do not match authoritative data, and certificate errors clustering around one name. Awareness means treating DNS as a security control with monitoring, not as plumbing that either works or does not.

SOLUTIONS. Cure and immunization: enable signed-answer validation on resolvers; use unpredictable source ports and query identifiers; prefer encrypted DNS transport where available; monitor high-value names for unexpected changes. Fix and response playbook: when poisoning is suspected, flush affected caches, verify answers against authoritative sources, check which users were misdirected and what they submitted, and rotate any credentials entered on a forged site. title: Supply-Chain Compromise
body:
EDUCATION. A supply-chain compromise attacks the trusted path between a maker and its users: instead of breaking into each victim, the attacker compromises a shared component, a build system, or an update channel, and the victims then install the compromise themselves because it arrives through a channel they trust. The power of the class is leverage: one compromised component reaches every user of that component. The defense is therefore verification at every handoff: artifacts must carry signatures from their maker, hashes that match published values, and provenance that names the build that produced them, and users must check those proofs before installing, especially for updates that arrive with unusual timing or content.

INFORMATION AWARENESS. Recognize the risk by its anomalies: an update that arrives outside the normal schedule, a component whose hash differs from the published value, a vendor announcement of a compromised build, and a new version whose contents do not match its release notes. Documented real cases include a 2020 network-management platform whose compromised update reached thousands of organizations, a 2023 file-transfer product mass-exploited through its own update path, and a 2023 communications product compromised through its installer. title: Business Email Compromise
body:
EDUCATION. Business email compromise is fraud conducted with a stolen or spoofed business identity: the attacker impersonates an executive, a supplier, or a trusted colleague and persuades finance staff to change payment details or send money to an attacker's account. It needs no malware and no technical flaw; it needs only a convincing message and a procedure that lets one email change where money goes. Variants include fake invoices, fake executive urgency, and fake supplier bank-detail changes. The defense is procedural: no payment destination changes on the strength of an email alone, ever. title: Denial-of-Service Exhaustion
body:
EDUCATION. A denial-of-service attack does not steal or alter data; it exhausts something the service needs, such as bandwidth, connections, or processing, until legitimate users cannot get through. Distributed variants summon traffic from many compromised devices at once, which is why blocking one source does not help. The attack works because most services are built for expected load, not adversarial load, and because some requests are cheap to send but expensive to answer. The defense is to make the service cheap to defend and expensive to exhaust: absorb traffic across many locations, rate-limit aggressively, cache aggressively, and hand the largest floods to an upstream provider built for them. Availability is a security property, not only a performance goal.

title: Insider Misuse and Data Exfiltration

title: AI Deepfake Impersonation

title: Drive-By Download and Watering Hole
body:

A drive-by download infects a visitor without any conscious action beyond visiting a page: the page, or an advertisement on it, exploits an unpatched browser or plugin, or tricks the visitor into running something.
